name: Arje
title: A person at Israel's court during King Pekahiah's reign, killed in Pekah's coup
summary: Arje is briefly mentioned in 2 Kings as a man who was killed along with King Pekahiah of Israel and another man named Argob, when Pekah son of Remaliah carried out his coup in the king's palace at Samaria. The biblical text gives no further details about Arje's position or role, but his presence in the palace at the time of the coup suggests an association with the king's inner circle. This event is part of a series of violent power shifts that characterized the northern kingdom of Israel during its final decade, a period marked by political instability and persistent idolatry among the nation's leaders. The textual uncertainty surrounding the verse where Arje is mentioned means his historical identity remains debated among biblical scholars.

keyEvents.title: Killed during Pekah's coup against King Pekahiah
keyEvents.description: Arje was killed along with King Pekahiah and Argob when Pekah, son of Remaliah, carried out a coup in the king's palace in Samaria with fifty men from Gilead. The event marked yet another violent transfer of power during the turbulent final phase of the northern kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Pekah's takeover following the assassination
keyEvents.description: After the killing of Pekahiah, Arje, and Argob, Pekah seized the throne and reigned as king over Israel. He too continued the idolatry that had characterized the kings of the northern kingdom.

versions.summary: Arje was a prominent figure at the court in Samaria who was killed together with King Pekahiah of Israel by Pekah, son of Remaliah, during the coup against the king. He is mentioned briefly in 2 Kings as a victim of the violent seizure of power in the northern kingdom of Israel.
versions.title: King of Judah who was murdered
versions.reason: [critical] The title says 'Judas king', but Arje was not a king at all, nor was he associated with Judah. He was a person at the court of Israel (the northern kingdom) who was killed during Pekah's coup against King Pekahja of Israel.; [major] The summary calls Arje 'a prominent figure at the court in Samaria', which is a reasonable interpretation, but it should be clarified that his exact role remains uncertain. The Hebrew text in 2 Kings 15:25 is disputed – some scholars suggest that Arje and Argob may have been Pekah's co-conspirators rather than victims of the coup. Nevertheless, the most common reading is that they were killed together with Pekahja.; [minor] The role 'leader' is very general and somewhat speculative. The biblical text provides little information about Arje's position. A more neutral description such as 'courtier' or 'person at Israel's court' would be more precise, possibly 'officer' if he is interpreted as a military figure.; [minor] The event 'Pekahja's short reign' primarily concerns Pekahja, not Arje directly. It is a reasonable contextual event, but the description 'Arje was associated with Pekahja's court' is an interpretation that goes beyond what the text explicitly states.; [minor] The event 'Unrest in the kingdom of Israel' is more of a historical context than a specific incident linked to Arje. The theological interpretation regarding 'God's judgment on the nation's apostasy' is reasonable, but should be presented with somewhat greater caution for such a briefly mentioned figure.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For such an obscure person as Arje, notes should be added concerning textual critical issues around 2 Kings 15:25, the meaning of the name, and the historical context.

Little is known about Arje's role or position, but his presence in the palace during the coup suggests an association with the king's inner circle. versions.reason: [minor] The title is clear, but could be refined to clarify that Ahijah was associated with the court of the northern kingdom of Israel.; [minor] Pekahiah reigned approximately 740–738 BC, so 'around the 700s BC' is technically correct, but it would be more precise to specify 'around the 740s BC'.; [minor] The role 'court official' is a reasonable assumption, but the text does not explicitly state Ahijah's position. It may be worth adding a more neutral description such as 'person at the king's court', or retaining 'court official' with a note about the uncertainty.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but the phrasing 'apostasy from God' in the final sentence could be nuanced. The text says that the kings 'did what was evil in the Lord's sight', which often refers to idolatry, but this was a persistent problem throughout the entire northern kingdom, not something specifically tied to Ahijah.; [minor] The second keyEvent ('Pekah's rise to power') focuses more on Pekah than on Ahijah. It is acceptable as context, but could be tightened to maintain focus on Ahijah's role in the event.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew text in 2 Kgs 15:25 is text-critically challenging. Some scholars suggest that the names Arje and Argob may originally have belonged to a gloss or another context, and were secondarily inserted into the verse. The Septuagint has a somewhat different reading of this verse, which reinforces the uncertainty surrounding the original text.

The name Arje (אַרְיֵה) means 'lion' in Hebrew. Lion names were common in ancient Israel and the Middle East, and may reflect a desire for strength and courage for the bearer. Similar animal names are found in several Semitic cultures.

The period around 740–730 BC was marked by great political instability in the northern kingdom of Israel. From the death of Jeroboam II until the fall of the kingdom in 722 BC, several kings were murdered by their successors. The growing power of Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III exerted strong external pressure on the small Levantine kingdoms and contributed to internal unrest.

The palace in Samaria, where the coup took place, is archaeologically linked to the Israelite palace on the hill of Samaria. Excavations have revealed impressive building remains from the Iron Age, including the famous ivory cache, which testifies to the wealth and power of the Israelite kings during this period.

Some scholars have suggested that Arje and Argob may have been military officers or bodyguards loyal to King Pekahiah, and that they were killed because they tried to defend the king during the coup. This interpretation is speculative, however, as the biblical text does not specify their roles.
